definition: Standard: nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort order. FIFO: strict order per message group, exactly-once processing, lower throughput, and the queue name ends in .fifo.
A receive call waits up to 20 seconds for a message instead of returning empty. Fewer API calls, lower cost and latency. Remember: many empty receives means enable long polling.
Receives messages that failed processing more than maxReceiveCount times, isolating poison messages for debugging. Redrive moves them back later. A FIFO queue needs a FIFO dead-letter queue.
Publish once to an SNS topic and every subscribed SQS queue gets its own copy. Each queue access policy must allow the topic. Remember: one S3 event, many consumers.
Real-time stream made of shards. Order is kept per partition key, retention is 24 hours by default and up to 365 days, and many consumers can replay data.
Fully managed, auto-scaling delivery of streaming data to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, Splunk or HTTP endpoints. Can transform with Lambda and convert to Parquet. Buffers data, no replay.
Managed Apache ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ brokers using open protocols like AMQP, MQTT and STOMP. Remember: migrate on-premises messaging without code changes. Scales less than SQS and SNS.

term: ECS Task Role vs Execution Role
definition: Task role: permissions your application code uses, set per task definition. Execution role: lets ECS pull images, send logs and read secrets. Remember: app calls S3, use the task role.
Decide where tasks run: Fargate, Fargate Spot or an EC2 Auto Scaling group. Managed scaling adds instances when tasks cannot be placed. Fargate Spot saves up to 70 percent.
Managed Kubernetes control plane. Pods run on managed node groups, self-managed EC2 nodes, Fargate, or EKS Auto Mode. Remember: already using Kubernetes or need cloud-agnostic tooling, choose EKS.
Deploys web apps from source code or a container with built-in scaling and HTTPS. Closed to new customers since April 30, 2026. AWS now points to Amazon ECS Express Mode.
Up to 15 minutes per invocation, memory 128 MB to 10 GB, temporary storage and container images up to 10 GB, and 1,000 concurrent executions per Region by default.

Reserved: guarantees and caps concurrency for one function, free. Provisioned: keeps environments initialized to remove cold starts, extra cost. Remember: throttling means reserved; cold starts means provisioned.
Snapshots the initialized function when a version is published, then resumes from that snapshot to cut cold starts. Supports Java, Python and .NET. No extra charge for Java.
CloudFront Functions: JavaScript, viewer events only, sub-millisecond, cheapest, no network calls. Lambda@Edge: Node.js or Python, viewer and origin events, longer runtime, network access allowed.
In-memory cache for DynamoDB giving microsecond reads through a compatible API, so little code change. Remember: DAX caches items and queries; ElastiCache suits computed aggregation results.
Deletes items automatically after the expiry timestamp in a chosen attribute passes, using no write capacity. Remember: session data or temporary records that should expire on their own.
IAM for AWS users and roles. Cognito user pool authorizer for app users. Lambda authorizer for custom or third-party tokens. Remember: API keys identify clients but do not authenticate them.
Standard: runs up to one year, exactly-once execution, suits long workflows and human approval. Express: up to five minutes, very high volume, cheaper for short bursts.
User pools: sign-up and sign-in, returning JWT tokens for API Gateway or ALB. Identity pools: exchange an identity for temporary AWS credentials to call S3 or DynamoDB directly.
A new user item in DynamoDB is captured by DynamoDB Streams, which triggers Lambda to send the email through Amazon SES. Asynchronous, with no change to the write path.
